case_name: Percept D'Mark (India) Pvt. Ltd. v. Zaheer Khan & Anr.

clause_a.label: Clause 31(a) and 31(b)
clause_a.text:
31. NEGOTIATION AND RIGHTS OF FIRST REFUSAL:
(a) NEGOTIATION: During the third contract year, and in any event not later than August 1st, 2003 the Parties shall meet to commence discussions with a view to the extension of their relationship beyond the Term. For sixty (60) days thereafter, Zaheer Khan, agrees to negotiate in good faith only with Percept, and not with any third party, concerning the right after the Term to the use of his endorsement or for the arrangement contemplated by this Agreement in association with any goods or services. Only after such one hundred and eighty (180) day period from the date of the last assignment, Zaheer Khan shall have the right to negotiate with other persons, subject however to sub-clause (b).
(b) FIRST REFUSAL: During the Term of the Agreement, prior to completion of the first negotiation period provided for in sub-clause (a) above, Zaheer Khan agrees not to accept any offer for his endorsement, promotion, advertising, or other affiliation with regard to any products or services. Thereafter, Zaheer Khan agrees not to accept any offer for his endorsement, promotion, advertising, or other affiliation with regard to any goods or services or for arrangement similar to the transaction hereunder without first providing Percept with written notice of such offer and all the material terms and conditions thereof and offering Percept the right to match the third party offer.

Percept shall thereafter have right, exercisable by written notice to Zaheer Khan within ten(10) days of receipt, to accept Zaheer Khan's offer on the same terms and conditions offered by such third party. If Percept does not accept Zaheer Khan's offer, Zaheer Khan shall thereafter have the right to enter into an agreement with such third party.

court_held: The right of first refusal in Clause 31(b) could operate only during the term; enforcing it after the agreement expired would be a restraint of trade, prima facie void under Section 27. The Court refused to restore the interim injunction, leaving the appellant to a damages claim.
notes: Clause text copied from the judgment as shown on Indian Kanoon (para beginning 'Clause 31 (a) and (b) is reproduced below'). The risk is a post-term survival of a ROFR/exclusivity covenant; the term (3 years from 30.10.2000) is described but not quoted, so it is not given as clause_b. This is an interim-relief ruling ('prima facie void'), not a final decree.

case_name: Superintendence Company of India (P) Ltd. v. Krishan Murgai

clause_a.label: Clause 10 (letter of appointment)
clause_a.text: 10. That you will not be permitted to join any firm of our competitors or run a business of your own in similarity as directly and/or indirectly, for a period of two years at the place of your last posting after you leave the Company.

court_held: The Court dismissed the employer's appeal and refused to enforce the two-year post-employment non-compete. The headnote records that the clause, read narrowly, did not apply where the employer had terminated the employee, and that a restraint this wide operating after employment ends is hit by Section 27.
statute: Indian Contract Act, 1872, Section 27; Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 42/57
notes: Clause text as quoted in A.P. Sen J.'s opinion. The judges reached the same result by partly different routes (construction of 'leave' vs. outright invalidity of post-service restraints under s.27); check the full text before citing a single ratio.

case_name: Niranjan Shankar Golikari v. Century Spinning and Mfg. Co. Ltd.

clause_a.label: Clause 17 (employment agreement)
clause_a.text: In the event of the employee leaving, abandoning or resigning the service of the company in breach of the terms of the agreement before the expiry of the said period of five years he shall not directly or indirectly engage in or carry on of his own accord or in partnership with others the business at present being carried on by the company and he shall not serve in any capacity, whatsoever or be associated with any person, firm or company carrying on such business for the remainder of the said period and in addition pay to the company as liquidated damages 'an amount equal to the salaries the employee would have received during the period of six months thereafter and shall further reimburse to the company any amount that the company may have spent on the employee's training.

court_held: A negative covenant that operates only during the term of employment is not a restraint of trade under Section 27; the injunction restraining the employee from working for a competitor for the rest of the five-year term was upheld.
notes: Negative example: an in-term restraint is enforceable. Contrast with superintendence_murgai_1980 and percept_dmark_2006 (post-term restraints). The stray opening quote mark before 'an amount' is as printed in the judgment.

case_name: Gujarat Bottling Co. Ltd. & Ors. v. The Coca Cola Co. & Ors.

clause_a.label: Paragraph 14 (negative stipulation), 1993 Agreement
clause_a.text: As such the Bottler covenants that the Bottler will not manufacture, bottle, sell, deal or otherwise be concerned with the products, beverages of any other brands or trade marks/trade names during the subsistenance of this Agreement including the period of one year's notice as contemplated in paragraph 21.

court_held: The negative covenant barring the bottler from dealing in other brands during the agreement, including the one-year notice period, operates only during the subsistence of the contract and is not a restraint of trade under Section 27; the High Court's interim injunction enforcing it was upheld.
notes: Negative example (in-term exclusivity in a franchise/bottling agreement). The spelling 'subsistenance' is as printed. Paragraph 21 (one-year termination notice) is only paraphrased in the judgment, so it is not reproduced.

case_name: M/s Kailash Nath Associates v. Delhi Development Authority & Anr.

clause_a.label: Auction terms, para 2(iv)
clause_a.text: (iv) In case of default, breach or non-compliance of any of the terms and conditions of the auction or mis -representation by the bidder and/or intending purchaser, the earnest money shall be forfeited.

court_held: Forfeiting earnest money under a concluded contract is governed by Section 74; it is allowed only as reasonable compensation where the other side has suffered loss. DDA, which suffered no loss (it re-auctioned at a much higher price), could not forfeit Rs. 78 lakh, and the refund was restored.
notes: The spacing 'mis -representation' is as printed. The earnest money was 25% of the bid. The Court also noted that forfeiture can be valid where the deposit is a true earnest in a public auction before acceptance; the holding turns on a concluded contract and no proven loss.

case_name: Maula Bux v. Union of India

clause_a.label: Clause 8 (supply contract)
clause_a.text:
The officer sanctioning the contract may rescind his contract by notice to me/us in writing :--
(i)
(ii)
(iii)
(iv) If I/we decline, neglect or delay to comply with any demand or requisition or in any other way fail to. perform or observe any condition of the contract.
(v)
(vi) In ease of such rescission, my/our security deposit (or such portion thereof as the officer sanctioning the contract shall consider fit or adequate) shall stand forfeited and be absolutely at the disposal of Government, without prejudice to any other remedy or action that the Government may have to take.

In the case of such rescission, the Government shall be entitled to recover from me/us on demand any extra expense the Government may be put to in obtaining supplies/services hereby agreed to be supplied, from elsewhere in any manner mentioned in clause 7(ii) hereof, for the remainder of the period for which this contract was entered into, without prejudice to any other remedy the Government may have.

court_held: Forfeiting a security deposit for breach is a stipulation by way of penalty under Section 74, so the Government could keep only reasonable compensation. Since it could have proved its loss and did not, it had to refund the deposits.
notes: Empty sub-clauses (i)-(iii) and (v), and the OCR-style errors 'In ease' and 'fail to.', are reproduced as printed on Indian Kanoon. The clause pairs forfeiture with a separate right to recover extra expense, so in substance it is double recovery.

case_name: Oil & Natural Gas Corporation Ltd. v. Saw Pipes Ltd.

clause_a.label: Clause 11(a) (Failure and Termination / Liquidated Damages)
clause_a.text:
11. Failure and Termination Clause/Liquidated Damages:-
Time and date of delivery shall be essence of the contract. If the contractor fails to deliver the stores, or any installment thereof within the period fixed for such delivery in the schedule or at any time repudiates the contract before the expiry of such period, the purchaser may, without prejudice to any other right or remedy, available to him to recover damages for breach of the contract:-
(a) Recovery from the contractor as agreed liquidated damages are not by way of penalty, a sum equivalent to 1% (one percent) of the contract price of the whole unit per week for such delay or part thereof (this is an agreed, genuine pre-estimate of damages duly agreed by the parties) which the contractor has failed to deliver within the period fixed for delivery in the schedule, where delivery thereof is accepted after expiry of the aforesaid period. It may be noted that such recovery of liquidated damages may be upto 10% of the contract price of whole unit of stores which the contractor has failed to deliver within the period fixed for delivery, or

court_held: The liquidated damages clause (1% per week, capped at 10%) was a genuine pre-estimate of loss. ONGC could recover it without proving actual loss, and the award that required proof of loss was set aside as patently illegal.
statute: Indian Contract Act, 1872, Sections 73-74; Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, Section 34
notes: Negative example (a capped, reasoned LD clause that was enforced). The judgment's extract jumps from (a) to a note marked (e); only (a) is reproduced. The page-break hyphen in 'pre-estimate' was joined. Later cases (Kailash Nath 2015) qualify Saw Pipes: LD is still capped at reasonable compensation, and loss need not be proved only where it is hard to prove.

case_name: Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Ltd. v. Brojo Nath Ganguly & Anr.

clause_a.label: Rule 9(i), Service Rules (incorporated into employment contract)
clause_a.text: (i) The employment of a permanent employee shall be subject to termination on three months' notice on either side. The notice shall be in writing on either side. The Company may pay the equivalent of three months' basic pay and dearness allowance, if any, in lieu of notice or may deduct a like amount when the employee has failed to give due notice.

court_held: Rule 9(i), which let a government company end a permanent employee's service on three months' notice without reason, was unconscionable in a contract between parties of grossly unequal bargaining power. It was held void under Section 23 as opposed to public policy, and also violated Article 14.
statute: Indian Contract Act, 1872, Section 23; Constitution of India, Article 14
notes: This is a standard-form clause in service rules of a state instrumentality, so the Article 14 limb does not carry over to purely private contracts. The unconscionability/Section 23 reasoning is the part relevant to commercial standard-form contracts.

case_name: Union of India & Anr. v. M/s IndusInd Bank Ltd. & Anr.

clause_a.label: Bank guarantee claim-period clause
clause_a.text: …. Unless a demand or claim under this guarantee is made against us within three months from the above date (i.e. On or before 30.4.97), all your rights under the said guarantee shall be forfeited and we shall be relieved and discharged from all liabilities hereunder.

court_held: The amended Section 28 (1997), which voids clauses that extinguish rights unless a claim is made within a set time, is not retrospective. The guarantees were executed before the amendment, so the unamended Section 28 applied and the clause was valid; the bank was discharged.
statute: Indian Contract Act, 1872, Section 28 (pre- and post-1997 amendment)
notes: CAUTION: expected_flag follows the court's result (clause upheld), but only because the pre-1997 law applied. Under the current Section 28, a clause extinguishing rights for failure to claim within a set period is void, except the 2013 proviso for bank guarantees with a claim period of at least one year. A modern reviewer should flag this pattern, so treat this as a temporal edge case, not a clean negative. The leading ellipsis is in the judgment's quotation.

case_name: Jagdish Chander v. Ramesh Chander & Ors.

clause_a.label: Clause 16 (partnership deed)
clause_a.text: 16) If during the continuance of the partnership or at any time afterwards any dispute touching the partnership arises between the partners, the same shall be mutually decided by the partners or shall be referred for arbitration if the parties so determine.

court_held: A clause that sends disputes to arbitration only 'if the parties so determine' shows no present intention to arbitrate; it is not an arbitration agreement under Section 7, so the court could not appoint an arbitrator under Section 11.
statute: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, Sections 7 and 11
notes: Outcome is 'other': the clause was held not to be an arbitration agreement at all (unenforceable as one), not struck down as void. This is a useful 'optional/permissive arbitration wording' pattern.

case_name: M/s N.N. Global Mercantile Pvt. Ltd. v. M/s Indo Unique Flame Ltd.
citation: (2021) 4 SCC 379 (3-judge); (2023) 7 SCC 1 (Constitution Bench); overruled by In re Interplay between Arbitration Agreements under the A&C Act 1996 and the Indian Stamp Act 1899, 2023 INSC 1066 (7-judge)

clause_a.label: Clause 10, Work Order dated 28.09.2015
clause_a.text: 10. Arbitration : In case of any dispute due to difference of opinion in interpretation of any clause or terms and conditions or meaning of the work or language the decision of the arbitrator appointed with mutual consent shall be treated as final and binding on both the parties.

court_held: The 2021 bench held the arbitration clause severable and enforceable despite the unstamped work order. The April 2023 Constitution Bench (3:2) held an arbitration agreement in an unstamped instrument cannot be acted on until stamped. In December 2023 a 7-judge bench overruled that: non-stamping is a curable defect, not a ground to refuse appointing an arbitrator.
statute: Indian Stamp Act, 1899, Sections 33-35; Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, Sections 8, 11 and 16
notes: Clause text verified in the 2021 judgment. The ground truth changed twice, so do not use this as a void/valid label. The risk (an insufficiently stamped instrument) is document-level, not visible in the clause text, so a clause-text model may legitimately miss it. The clause is also loosely drafted (no seat, no appointment fallback).

case_name: Perkins Eastman Architects DPC & Anr. v. HSCC (India) Ltd.

clause_a.label: Clause 24.1(ii) (Dispute Resolution)
clause_a.text: (ii) Except where the decision has become final, binding and conclusive in terms of sub-Para (i) above disputes or difference shall be referred for adjudication through arbitration by a sole arbitrator appointed by the CMD HSCC within 30 days form the receipt of request from the Design Consultant. If the arbitrator so appointed is unable or unwilling to act or resigns his appointment or vacates his office due to any reason, whatsoever another sole arbitrator shall be appointed in the manner aforesaid. Such person shall be entitled to proceed with the reference from the reference from the stage at which it was left by his predecessor. It is a term of this contract that the party invoking arbitration shall give a list of disputes with amounts claimed in respect of each such dispute along with the notice for appointment of arbitrator and giving reference to the rejection by the CMD, HSCC of the appeal. It is also a term of this contract that no person other than a person appointed by such CMD, HSCC as aforesaid should act as arbitrator.

court_held: A party (or its officer) with an interest in the outcome, who is ineligible to be an arbitrator under Section 12(5), cannot unilaterally appoint a sole arbitrator either. The CMD's power to appoint was therefore unenforceable, and the Supreme Court appointed an independent sole arbitrator under Section 11.
statute: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, Section 11 and Section 12(5) read with the Seventh Schedule
notes: Excerpt is the contiguous sub-para (ii) as quoted; the clause continues with a sentence on applicability of the 1996 Act. Typos 'form the receipt' and the duplicated 'from the reference' are as printed. The CORE v. ECI SPIC line of cases (2019; Constitution Bench 2024) also concerns unilateral or panel-based appointment.

case_name: TRF Ltd. v. Energo Engineering Projects Ltd.

clause_a.label: Clause 33(d), GTCPO
clause_a.text: d. Unless otherwise provided, any dispute or difference between the parties in connection with this agreement shall be referred to sole arbitration of the Managing Director of Buyer or his nominee. Venue of arbitration shall be Delhi, and the arbitration shall be conducted in English language.

clause_b.label: Clause 33(c), GTCPO
clause_b.text: c. All disputes which cannot be settled by mutual negotiation shall be referred to and determined by arbitration as per the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 as amended.

court_held: Clause 33(c) made the amended Act (2015 amendment) applicable, under which the Managing Director is ineligible to act as arbitrator (Section 12(5), Seventh Schedule). Once he was ineligible, he could not nominate anyone either, so his nominee's appointment was set aside and the matter remitted for a fresh appointment.
statute: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, Section 12(5) read with the Seventh Schedule (as amended in 2015)
notes: Cross-clause: the 'as amended' statutory reference in 33(c) is what defeats the unilateral appointment mechanism in 33(d).

case_name: Enercon (India) Ltd. & Ors. v. Enercon GmbH & Anr.

clause_a.label: Clause 18.3, IPLA (venue London; Indian Act to apply)
clause_a.text:
18.3 A proceedings in such arbitration shall be conducted in English. The venue of the arbitration proceedings shall be in London. The arbitrators may (but shall not be obliged to) award costs and reasonable expenses (including reasonable-fees of counsel) to the Party (ies) that substantially prevail on merit.

The provisions of Indian Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 shall apply.

clause_b.label: Clause 17.1, IPLA (governing law)
clause_b.text: 17 GOVERNING LAW 17.1 This Agreement and any dispute of claims arising out of or in connection with its subject matter are governed by and construed in accordance with the Law of India.

court_held: Read with Indian governing law and the express application of the Indian Arbitration Act, 'venue ... London' named only a venue, not the seat. The seat was India, so Indian courts had supervisory jurisdiction. The Court also cured the unworkable appointment mechanism in 18.1 (the licensor's own arbitrator presiding) rather than declaring the clause inoperable.
statute: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, Part I (Sections 2(2), 20, 45)
notes: Classic seat/venue/governing-law inconsistency. Clause 18.1 (three arbitrators, licensor's appointee to preside) is also quoted in the judgment and could serve as a second clause_b if needed.

case_name: Union of India v. Hardy Exploration and Production (India) Inc.

clause_a.label: Article 33.12, Production Sharing Contract (venue)
clause_a.text: 33.12 The venue of conciliation or arbitration proceedings pursuant to this Article unless the parties otherwise agree, shall be Kuala Lumpur and shall be conducted in English language. Insofar as practicable the parties shall continue to implement the terms of this contract notwithstanding the initiation of arbitration proceedings and any pending claim or dispute.

clause_b.label: Article 32.1, Production Sharing Contract (governing law)
clause_b.text: 32.1 This Contract shall be governed and interpreted in accordance with the laws of India.

court_held: Kuala Lumpur was only the venue. With no seat agreed and none determined by the tribunal (the award being signed there did not make it the seat), and with Indian governing law, Indian courts had jurisdiction to hear the Section 34 challenge. The appeal of the Union of India was allowed.
statute: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, Sections 2(2), 20, 34; UNCITRAL Model Law Article 20
notes: Article 33.9 (UNCITRAL Model Law to govern, Article 33 prevails on conflict) is also quoted and part of the court's reasoning. BGS SGS Soma (2019) later criticised Hardy's reasoning on venue vs seat, so use it for the clause pattern, not as settled law.

case_name: BGS SGS Soma JV v. NHPC Ltd.

clause_a.label: Clause 67.3(vi)
clause_a.text: (vi) Arbitration Proceedings shall be held at New Delhi/Faridabad, India and the language of the arbitration proceedings and that of all documents and communications between the parties shall be English.

court_held: Where an arbitration clause names a 'venue' and nothing points the other way, the venue is the seat. Because all sittings and the award were in New Delhi, New Delhi was the seat, and only New Delhi courts could hear the Section 34 challenge, not Faridabad.
notes: The judgment is a PDF-derived text; the line-break hyphen in 'lan-guage' was joined, with no other change. The risk is naming two alternative places ('New Delhi/Faridabad') without designating a seat. The full Clause 67.3 (sub-clauses (i)-(vii)) is quoted at para 3.

case_name: Mankastu Impex Pvt. Ltd. v. Airvisual Ltd.

clause_a.label: Clause 17.2, MoU (arbitration administered in Hong Kong)
clause_a.text:
17.2 Any dispute, controversy, difference or claim arising out of or relating to this MoU, including the existence, validity, interpretation, performance, breach or termination thereof or any dispute regarding non-contractual obligations arising out of or relating to it shall be referred to and finally resolved by arbitration administered in Hong Kong.

The place of arbitration shall be Hong Kong.

The number of arbitrators shall be one. The arbitration proceedings shall be conducted in English language.

clause_b.label: Clause 17.1, MoU (governing law and court jurisdiction)
clause_b.text: 17.1 This MoU is governed by the laws of India, without regard to its conflicts of laws provisions and courts at New Delhi shall have the jurisdiction.

court_held: Hong Kong was the seat: arbitration 'administered in Hong Kong', with Hong Kong as the place. Clause 17.1 (Indian law and New Delhi courts) did not make India the seat; it covered the governing law and limited court functions such as interim relief and enforcement. The Section 11 petition was dismissed.
notes: Classic cross-clause pair: a foreign seat in the arbitration clause against an Indian exclusive-jurisdiction clause. Clause 17.3 (interim relief from a court having jurisdiction) was also quoted and used by the Court to reconcile the two.

case_name: M/s Swastik Gases (P) Ltd. v. Indian Oil Corporation Ltd.

clause_a.label: Clause 18.0 (Jurisdiction)
clause_a.text: 18.0. Jurisdiction The Agreement shall be subject to jurisdiction of the courts at Kolkata.

clause_b.label: Clause 17.0 (Arbitration)
clause_b.text: 17.0. Arbitration If any dispute or difference(s) of any kind whatsoever shall arise between the parties hereto in connection with or arising out of this Agreement, the parties hereto shall in good faith negotiate with a view to arriving at an amicable resolution and settlement. In the event no settlement is reached within a period of 30 days from the date of arising of the dispute(s)/difference(s), such dispute(s)/difference(s) shall be referred to 2 (two) Arbitrators, appointed one each by the parties and the Arbitrators, so appointed shall be entitled to appoint a third Arbitrator who shall act as a presiding Arbitrator and the proceedings thereof shall be in accordance with the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 or any statutory modification or re-enactment thereof in force. The existence of any dispute(s)/difference(s) or initiation/continuation of arbitration proceedings shall not permit the parties to postpone or delay the performance of or to abstain from performing their obligations pursuant to this Agreement.

court_held: Even without words like 'only' or 'exclusive', the jurisdiction clause naming Kolkata showed an intention to exclude other courts. It was valid under Section 28, so the Section 11 application belonged in Calcutta, not Rajasthan, where part of the cause of action arose.
statute: Indian Contract Act, 1872, Section 28; Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, Sections 2(1)(e), 11
notes: Negative example: a jurisdiction clause read with the arbitration clause and enforced as exclusive. Useful to test that a model does not over-flag a single-forum jurisdiction clause as an unlawful ouster under Section 28.
